query: Identify a processing route and property optimization strategy for a lightweight, multi-principal element alloy system. The goal is to achieve high density and hardness while ensuring resistance to high-temperature oxidation and aqueous corrosion. Request a hypothesis for the material composition and processing method, supporting evidence on phase stability, boundary conditions for the processing temperature, and a falsification experiment to test the mechanism of property enhancement.

generation.target_system: Lightweight, multi-principal element alloy (MPEA) system designed for high density (via refractory elements), high hardness, and resistance to high-temperature oxidation and aqueous corrosion. Target composition family: Al-free, Cr-rich, refractory-based BCC HEA (e.g., Cr-Mo-Nb-W-V or Cr-Mo-Nb-W-Ti variants). Target processing state: Dense bulk via Spark Plasma Sintering (SPS) of mechanically alloyed powders.

evidence_appraisal.record_system: Al-Co-Fe-Ni-Cr high entropy alloy (AlCoFeNi vs AlCo0.5Cr0.5FeNi)
evidence_appraisal.difference_from_target: Target requires high density and oxidation resistance; this record focuses on Al-containing systems which are lightweight but prone to oxidation issues if Al is depleted or if B2 decomposition occurs. The target system seeks to avoid Al to maximize density and potentially improve oxidation stability via Cr-rich oxides without the volatility risks of Al2O3 in certain environments, or to use Al strategically. More critically, the target seeks high hardness via BCC, while this record discusses B2/BCC decomposition in Al-rich systems.
evidence_appraisal.reason: The mechanism of phase decomposition (B2 + BCC) and the influence of Cr substitution on magnetism and hardness transfer to the design logic of phase control. However, the Al-rich composition is not the target; the target is a lightweight (but high density) refractory system. The principle of using Cr to tune phase stability and hardness is transferable.

generation.hypothesis: A lightweight (relative to W-based superalloys) but high-density refractory multi-principal element alloy (MPEA) with a composition of Cr-Mo-Nb-W-V (or Cr-Mo-Nb-W-Ti for slight density reduction) processed via Mechanical Alloying (MA) followed by Spark Plasma Sintering (SPS) at 1200–1400 °C will achieve a single-phase or BCC + Laves phase microstructure with nanocrystalline grain sizes (<100 nm). This processing route will induce severe lattice distortion and precipitation hardening, resulting in high hardness (>600 Hv) and compressive strength (>2500 MPa). The high Cr content will ensure the formation of a stable, self-healing Cr2O3 oxide layer at high temperatures, providing resistance to oxidation and aqueous corrosion, while the refractory elements (Nb, W, Mo) provide high-temperature strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Elemental powders of Cr, Mo, Nb, W, and V (or Ti) in near-equiatomic or slightly off-equiatomic ratios (e.g., Cr25Mo20Nb20W20V15 at%).
generation.intervention: Mechanical Alloying (MA) of elemental powders for 20–40 hours to form a supersaturated BCC solid solution with nanocrystalline grain size (<50 nm), followed by Spark Plasma Sintering (SPS) at 1200–1400 °C under vacuum or inert atmosphere for 10–30 minutes to achieve >98% relative density.
generation.conditions: MA: Ball-to-powder ratio 10:1, rotation speed 300 rpm, inert gas atmosphere. SPS: Temperature 1200–1400 °C, pressure 50 MPa, heating rate 100 °C/min, dwell time 10–30 min.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanocrystalline BCC solid solution matrix with potential fine Laves phase precipitates (e.g., Cr2Nb) at grain boundaries or within grains, and a surface Cr2O3 oxide layer formed during high-temperature exposure.
generation.mechanism: The mechanism relies on the severe lattice distortion from the multi-principal element mixing (cocktail effect) and the grain boundary strengthening from the nanocrystalline structure achieved via MA. The SPS process preserves this fine microstructure while densifying the material. The high hardness and strength are driven by the BCC structure and precipitation hardening (Laves phases). The oxidation and corrosion resistance are driven by the preferential formation of a dense, protective Cr2O3 layer, as supported by the general principle of Cr-rich alloys forming protective oxides, while avoiding Mn (which forms non-protective oxides) and Al (which may be volatile or lead to different phase stability issues in this specific high-density context).
generation.predicted_outcome: Vickers hardness: 650–750 Hv. Compressive strength: 2600–2900 MPa. Oxidation resistance: Minimal weight gain after 100 hours at 800 °C due to Cr2O3 layer. Corrosion resistance: Low corrosion current density in H2SO4 solution, comparable to or better than conventional wear-resistant composites.
generation.baseline: Conventional refractory HEAs produced by vacuum arc melting (e.g., NbMoTaW) which often suffer from coarse microstructures and lower hardness, or Ni-based superalloys which are heavier and less corrosion-resistant in certain aggressive environments.
generation.boundary: The process is limited to temperatures below 1400 °C to prevent excessive grain coarsening and Laves phase dissolution. The composition must maintain a high Cr content (>20 at%) to ensure oxidation resistance. The system is not suitable for applications requiring high ductility, as the BCC structure and nanocrystalline nature favor high strength over ductility.
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainty exists regarding the exact phase stability at the lower end of the SPS temperature range (1200 °C) where Laves phase precipitation might be incomplete or excessive. The long-term stability of the Cr2O3 layer in highly aggressive aqueous environments (e.g., high chloride) is less certain than in H2SO4. The density of the alloy will be high (~10.5 g/cm3), which may conflict with a strict
generation.lightweight: definition if the target was meant to be <8 g/cm3, but it is lighter than W-based superalloys.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate a Cr-Mo-Nb-W-V HEA via MA+SPS at 1200 °C and 1400 °C. Subject the samples to high-temperature oxidation (800 °C, 100 h) and electrochemical corrosion in 1M H2SO4. Compare the microstructure (XRD, SEM) and oxide layer composition (XPS) with the predicted BCC+Laves structure and Cr2O3 layer.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if: (1) The SPS process at 1200–1400 °C results in a predominantly FCC structure or coarse grains (>500 nm) instead of nanocrystalline BCC; (2) The hardness is below 500 Hv; (3) The oxidation test shows significant weight gain (>10 mg/cm2) or the formation of non-protective oxides (e.g., Mn oxides if Mn were present, or volatile oxides); (4) The corrosion resistance is significantly lower than the baseline refractory HEAs (e.g., >10x higher corrosion current density).

cited_evidence.text: This paper utilizes in situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) to investigate the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (HEA). We found that (1) Mn is the major oxide-forming element in both vacuum and air environments, leading to the formation of non-protective oxides that deplete the bulk alloy of Mn; (2) no oxides like Cr 2 O 3 , Fe 2 O 3 , or Fe 3 O 4 were observed during the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi, which contradicts some previous studies on the isothermal oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi HEA. We also analysed and compared the experimental results with thermodynamic calculations by using ThermoCalc version 2022b software following the CALPHAD method. ThermoCalc predicted spinel oxide in a vacuum environment, along with halite oxides observed in experimental results; also, in an atmospheric environment, it predicted only spinel, indicating the need for further investigation into factors to validate the thermodynamic predictions. In this paper, the impact of mechanical alloying (MA) and spark plasma sintering (SPS) on the phase evolution and mechanical properties development of CoCrFeNiTi high–entropy alloys (HEAs) was investigated. The microstructure and properties of the material were examined, using X-ray diffraction (XRD) for phase identification, scanning electron microscopy (SEM) for surface morphology observation, transmission electron microscopy (TEM) for microstructural analysis, and hardness testing to evaluate mechanical performance. The milled powder exhibited nanocrystalline solid solution microstructure with grain sizes below 48 nm, composed of 83% face–centered cubic (FCC) and 17% body–centered cubic (BCC) phases. Mechanically, the bulk CoCrFeNiTi alloy exhibited exceptional strength attributes, as evidenced by a Vickers hardness value reaching 675 Hv, along with a compressive strength of 1894 MPa and a yield stress of 1238 MPa. Refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) have excellent mechanical properties, which could make them the substitutes of some superalloys. However, the high melting point of refractory HEAs leads to processing problems when using traditional processing techniques. In this study, a single BCC solid solution of NbMoTaW alloy was formed by selective laser melting (SLM) with a linear energy density of up to 2.83 J/mm. The composition distribution was analyzed, and the element with a lower melting point and lower density showed a negative deviation (no more than 5%) of the molar ratio in the formed alloy. The HEA shows an excellent microstructure, microhardness, and corrosion resistance performance compared with traditional superalloys, making it a new substitute metal with great application prospects in aerospace and energy fields.

Corrosion resistance of alloys in light water reactors (LWRs) and more generally in oxidative environments is achieved by the formation of protective oxide layers that hinder further oxidation. Alloys containing Cr, Al, or Si typically tend to form a compact and self-healing chromia (Cr 2 O 3 ), alumina (Al 2 O 3 ) or silica (SiO 2 ) layers, respectively, which acts as effective diffusion barriers against further oxidation [1] – [3] . However, in molten fluoride salts (salt of choice for many molten salt reactor concepts, MSRs) these protective oxide layers on structural alloys are unstable which in turn leads to the dissolution of the least noble element in the alloy. Such a corrosion mechanism can lead to a reduction in components’ wall thickness and eventually the loss of the structural integrity of the reactor components [1] , [2] . The dissolution products themselves may lead to plate-out in the relatively cooler sections of the system due to the strong sensitivity of solubility of analytes to temperature.

In this study, bulk samples of a CrMoNbWV high-entropy alloy (HEA) were obtained for the first time by spark plasma sintering (SPS) of mechanically alloyed (MA) powders at 1200 °C, 1300 °C, and 1400 °C. Microstructure evolution, phase formation as well as wear and corrosion behavior were investigated. The MA powders’ phase composition was found to be represented by body-centered-cubic (BCC) solid solution. The solid solution partially decomposed to Laves phases under the sintering, such as Cr 2 Nb and (Fe, Cr)Nb, and NbVO 4 -VO oxides mixture. The temperature increase to 1400 °C led to a grain coarsening of the BCC phase and decreased the Laves phase content accompanied by precipitation at the grain boundaries. The sintered samples showed high hardness and compressive strength (2700–2800 MPa) at room temperature. The wear tests demonstrated excellent results in comparison to conventional wear-resistant composites. The obtained samples also exhibited high corrosion resistance under electrochemical tests in H 2 SO 4 solution.
